strengths: Clear problem formulation: Identifies genuine feature entanglement issue in prior trajectory-controlled methods with effective visual evidence (Figure 2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple metrics (FVD, PSNR, SSIM, VBench), trajectory accuracy, user study, ablations, and in-the-wild generalization tests
Consistent empirical improvements: Across all evaluation metrics with user study showing 47.33% preference vs. 20.61% for second-best baseline
Intuitive and well-motivated design: Phase-wise decomposition with phase-specific dominant objects is conceptually sound and simplifies annotation
Practical robustness: Mask-based representation robust to incomplete input (97.89-99.81% PSNR at 60-90% sparsity); more user-friendly than point-based methods
Clear presentation and visualization: Well-structured paper with effective figures clearly communicating key concepts
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution is decomposing interaction into phases and selecting phase-specific objects—primarily an engineering insight. Subject representation (Eq. 3-4) uses straightforward pooling + circular expansion; motion injector (Eq. 6) is simple additive fusion

Weak theoretical justification: Why phase decomposition solves 'feature entanglement' is not rigorously analyzed. Robot arm still exists during interaction phase; unclear why object trajectory alone suffices. Intuition is domain-specific and may not generalize
Modest improvements without statistical validation: FVD ~3% improvement, trajectory error ~9%, user study margin only 47.33% vs. 20.61%. No confidence intervals or significance testing reported

Missing critical downstream validation: No evaluation of whether generated videos improve robot policy learning—the stated primary motivation. Relies on proxy metrics (FVD, trajectory accuracy) that may not correlate with actual utility

Narrow scope and limited generalization: Single-object, tabletop manipulation with grippers. Only trained on Bridge V2. In-the-wild tests still on similar gripper scenarios. Unclear scalability to multi-step or multi-object tasks

Incomplete ablation studies: 'w/o Causal Embedding' conflates multiple factors. Cross-attention baseline lacks explanation for poor performance. No ablation on circular volume design choices (why circular vs. other shapes?)

Design choices lack justification: Circular volumetric representation with radius ∝ Σm[i,j] is heuristic without principled rationale. Why this decomposition vs. alternative multi-modal fusion approaches (e.g., hierarchical trajectory space decomposition)?
Insufficient user study details: Only preference percentages reported; missing number of participants, study protocol, inter-rater agreement, and evaluation criteria
Limited failure analysis: Acknowledged issues with out-of-domain objects and 2D-only representation lack systematic investigation of when/why decomposition fails
Reproducibility concerns: No code availability mentioned; depends on pre-trained CogVideoX-5B; annotation pipeline sensitivity to hyperparameters (motion threshold τ) not thoroughly explored

weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Individual components are straightforward—circular volumetric pooling (Eq. 4), additive motion injection (Eq. 6), and latent propagation lack technical depth
Primarily engineering contribution: The core idea is problem decomposition and system design rather than novel methods; combination of existing techniques is sensible but incremental
Modest quantitative improvements: Many gains are 1-3% (FVD 3.2%, PSNR 1.5%, SSIM 1.9%), though trajectory error improvements are more substantial
Incomplete core validation: No rigorous demonstration that feature entanglement is prevented; lacks explicit interaction fidelity metrics or visualization of feature maps to support key claims
Motivation-to-evaluation gap: Paper motivates work for robot learning but only demonstrates improved video quality; no validation on actual sim-to-real transfer or policy learning
Limited experimental scope: Only Bridge V2 + in-the-wild images (same domain), 214 test samples, no cross-dataset evaluation or comparison with general video methods
Insufficient technical justification: Design choices unexplained (e.g., why radius ∝ mask area? why simple addition works?); causality property asserted without rigorous definition
Weak ablation on core contribution: Table 4 includes separate trajectories ablation but lacks systematic isolation of collaborative trajectory benefits or design alternatives

Vague problem formulation: 'Feature entanglement' is intuitive but not formally defined; mechanism by which phase decomposition prevents fusion issues unexplained
Evaluation metrics limitations: Trajectory error (L1 distance) crude for interaction quality; user study lacks details (inter-rater reliability, sample size per comparison)

weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution (decomposing trajectory by interaction phase) is incremental over Tora; motion injector uses standard convolutions; no architectural innovations versus base CogVideoX

Small test set: Only 214 samples on Bridge dataset insufficient for robust generalization claims

Significant acknowledged generalization limitations: Grounded-SAM success rates 0.67 (single object) and 0.14 (multi-object); cannot generalize to novel robot morphologies; poor performance on complex multi-object scenarios

strengths: Clear problem identification and well-motivated solution: The paper effectively identifies feature entanglement in overlapping regions when separately modeling robot and object trajectories, with compelling visual evidence (Fig. 2).
Novel collaborative trajectory formulation: Decomposing interaction into phases and using different dominant agents is intuitive, physically motivated, and distinct from prior work.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Evaluation across three benchmarks (Bridge, RLBench, SIMPLER) with multiple metrics (FVD, PSNR, SSIM, trajectory error, user preference, downstream action planning), demonstrating consistent improvements.

Practical usability and robustness: Mask-based representation is more user-friendly than points; users only annotate objects and phases rather than full trajectories; graceful degradation with sparse masks (60%) and imperfect prompts (40%).
Thorough ablation studies: Systematic analysis of causal embedding, representation choices, trajectory decomposition, and robustness to various input perturbations.

Strong empirical results on video quality and trajectory accuracy: Consistent improvements over Tora (FVD 147.31→152.28, object trajectory error 24.16→26.43) and significant user preference (45.16% vs 17.74%).
Out-of-domain generalization: Demonstrates capability on diverse unseen objects (bee, dumpling, lobster) despite training on single dataset.
Dataset contribution: 21k annotated video-trajectory samples with human-in-the-loop quality control pipeline.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Subject embeddings are straightforward (masked feature extraction + circular volumes); motion injector is simple additive injection. Core contribution is problem formulation rather than novel technical components.

Insufficient theoretical justification: Why does using object trajectory specifically address feature entanglement? Causal representation approach lacks motivation. Limited analysis of alternative formulations or ablations on mechanism design.

Dataset and comparison concerns: All baselines retrained on authors' curated data—advantage may come from data quality rather than method. No direct comparison with baselines on original data. Annotation pipeline required 4k manual corrections (Grounded-SAM success rate only 0.67).

Modest downstream task improvements: Action planning success rates often marginal over Tora (e.g., 0.83 vs 0.79 on pick cup, but Tora better on put knife at 0.82 vs 0.76). Only 100 episodes per task without confidence intervals. Unclear if video quality gains translate to consistent utility.
Small evaluation scale: Test set of 214 samples; user study details missing (rater count, inter-rater agreement); standard video metrics (FVD, PSNR) known to be noisy.
Generalization limitations: Requires post-training on 1,300 task-specific samples for RLBench/SIMPLER; poor generalization to novel robot morphologies; 2D-only control limits applicability.
Simple motion injector design: Additive fusion without justification for design choice; ablation shows cross-attention worse but lacks analysis; zero-initialization not motivated.
Limited failure analysis: No concrete failure examples, analysis of when collaborative trajectory helps/hurts, or discussion of challenging interaction types.
Reproducibility concerns: No code release mentioned; complex annotation pipeline hard to reproduce; some design choices appear arbitrary (radius ∝ mask area).
Missing comparisons: No evaluation against recent video diffusion models or other interaction-aware architectures.
